questions.question: If $M_X$ is finite on an open interval around $0$, how is the $n$th moment $\mathbb{E}[X^n]$ obtained from it?
A random variable $X$ has an MGF finite for every $|t|<\tfrac{1}{10}$. Which conclusion is guaranteed, even if $X$ is unbounded?
options: Only its first absolute moment is guaranteed to be finite.
Only its first two absolute moments are guaranteed to be finite.
Every absolute moment $\mathbb{E}[|X|^n]$, for integer $n\geq1$, is finite.
Its moments are guaranteed to be finite only if its support is bounded.

questions.question: Which expression gives $\operatorname{Var}(X)$ in terms of the MGF?
In deriving moments from $M_X(t)=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{tX}]$, why assume that $M_X$ is finite on an open interval around $0$?
options: To ensure that the random variable has bounded support.
To ensure that the value $M_X(0)$ is finite.
To identify moments with the values $M_X(1),M_X(2),\ldots$.
To justify passing derivatives inside the expectation.

questions.question: An MGF is finite for $-2<t<2$. Differentiating under expectation gives $M_X''(t)=\mathbb{E}[X^2\mathrm{e}^{tX}]$. What does $M_X''(-1)$ represent?
A random variable has $M_X(t)=\mathrm{e}^{3t+2t^2}$. What is $\mathbb{E}X$?
An MGF $M_X(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-t+5t^2/2}$ has $M_X'(0)=-1$ and $M_X''(0)=6$. What is $\operatorname{Var}(X)$?
Let $M_X(t)=\tfrac12+\tfrac14\mathrm{e}^{t}+\tfrac14\mathrm{e}^{2t}$. Differentiating, what is $\mathbb{E}X$?
For $M_X(t)=(1-2t)^{-3}$, $t<\tfrac12$, what is $\mathbb{E}X$?

Suppose $M_X(t)=\mathrm{e}^{5t}M_Z(t)$, with $M_Z(0)=1$, $M_Z'(0)=0$ and $M_Z''(0)=1$. The product rule gives $M_X''(t)=\mathrm{e}^{5t}\big(25M_Z(t)+10M_Z'(t)+M_Z''(t)\big)$. What is $\mathbb{E}[X^2]$?
An MGF has Taylor expansion $M_X(t)=1+at+bt^2+ct^3+\cdots$ near zero. A student claims that $\mathbb{E}[X^3]=c$ because $c$ multiplies $t^3$. Which correction is needed?
A random variable satisfies $\mathbb{E}|X|<\infty$ but $M_X(t)=\infty$ for every $t\ne0$. Can the MGF identity $\mathbb{E}X=M_X'(0)$ be used to obtain its mean?
options: No; the mean must also be infinite.
No; finiteness of the MGF around zero is missing.
Yes; a finite one-sided derivative still gives the mean.

questions.question: Let $K(t)=\ln M_X(t)$ near $0$. What are $K'(0)$ and $K''(0)$?
For $X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(2,p)$, where $0<p<1$, the MGF is $M_X(t)=(1-p+p\mathrm{e}^t)^2$. Differentiating twice, what is $\mathbb{E}[X^2]$?
A waiting time has $M_X(t)=\mathrm{e}^{t}/(1-2t)$ for $t<\tfrac12$. Let $K(t)=\ln M_X(t)$; you may use $\mathbb{E}X=K'(0)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=K''(0)$. What are its mean and variance?
Near $0$, an MGF expands as $M_X(t)=1+2t+3t^2+\cdots$. What is $\operatorname{Var}(X)$?
Two random variables have MGFs with the same derivatives of every order at $0$, both finite on an open interval around $0$. What follows?
options: Equal moments of every order, and the same law
The same mean, but possibly different variances
The two variables are equal as random variables
Nothing: derivatives at one point say too little

questions.question: For $X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1)$, $M_X(t)=(1-t)^{-1}=\sum_{n\geq0}t^n$ for $|t|<1$. A student sets $Y=X-\mathbb{E}X$ and claims that centring makes every odd moment zero. Which pair of moments assesses this claim?
A random variable has MGF $M_X(t)=\mathrm{e}^{t+t^2/2}=1+t+t^2+\tfrac23t^3+\tfrac5{12}t^4+\cdots$ near zero. What is its fourth central moment $\mathbb{E}[(X-\mathbb{E}X)^4]$?
An equal mixture of two normal laws has $M_X(t)=\tfrac12\mathrm{e}^{t^2/2}+\tfrac12\mathrm{e}^{2t+t^2/2}$. Find $\operatorname{Var}(X)$ from the derivatives at $0$.
